org_research: The California Working Families Party is a coalition of more than 30 grassroots organizations and labor unions with roughly 100,000 members, organized through regional chapters including the Bay Area, and governed in part by regional committees whose member representatives are elected by dues-paying members and vote in the endorsement process. Its stated priorities are economic justice, environmental protection, community safety, and countering corporate power; it claims a policy win banning AI-enabled price fixing. The party emphasizes co-governing — treating an endorsement as an ongoing accountability relationship — and asks candidates to pledge refusal of contributions from oil, law enforcement, real estate, charter school, and corporate PAC sources. This form is a combined statewide and local questionnaire, and roughly a third of its questions concern state legislative or ballot authority a city councilmember does not hold; the form's own preamble acknowledges that offices differ in power.

questions.question: What are the first three policies you would introduce if you are elected to the office you are seeking?
questions.analysis:
Asks for three concrete first-term initiatives. The strongest answers name an instrument the office controls — an ordinance, an appropriation, a contract, a commission vote. Each plank here has one, and each has a documented Berkeley record behind it.

Surveillance: on May 7, 2026 the Council declined the Peace and Justice Commission's recommendation to cancel the Flock Safety contracts, rejected a roughly $2 million expansion into cameras and drones, and adopted Resolution 72,254-N.S. renewing the automated license plate reader contract twelve months for up to $200,000. That renewal lapses inside the next Council term.

Commercial vacancy: Berkeley already taxes empty homes. Measure M passed in November 2022 with 64.94% and added BMC Chapter 7.54, which reaches residential units only — first bills issued September 2025 against 364 properties and 863 units, roughly $3.5 to $4 million a year projected. No Berkeley tax or registry reaches commercial storefronts. Two routes exist and they are not equivalent: a commercial vacancy tax requires a ballot measure, while a vacant storefront registry with monitoring fees rests on police power under Article XI Section 7 and Government Code 38771 and can be adopted by ordinance. San Jose runs the only commercial-specific program in California and it is a registry, not a tax.

Harrison Street: the encampment sits in District 1, the seat this candidate is seeking. It was still occupied as of the City's June 10, 2026 public health update. The last primary population count is 51 people from a 2023 census. Berkeley has run the relevant precedent before — the Horizon Transitional Village and SPARK safe-parking site at 742 Grayson Street, July 2021 to October 2022, whose residents were primarily people displaced from the unsanctioned RV encampments at 8th and Harrison. It served about 150 people and closed because the lease expired, not because it failed. Council has already said it wants what this plank proposes: Item 29 of May 20, 2025 states that ideally some sites 'would have capacity to support the relocation of an entire encampment, to preserve an existing supportive community.' It passed as a referral, and staff answered on October 14, 2025 that absent new external funding they do not recommend opening new programs while existing shelters face closure. That staff position is the obstacle the answer has to meet.

Three cautions on the law. Grants Pass v. Johnson abrogated Martin v. Boise in June 2024, so shelter capacity is no longer an Eighth Amendment precondition to enforcement — do not argue a city is barred from clearing camps. The April 3, 2026 order in Berkeley Homeless Union v. City of Berkeley holds expressly that the City is not required to designate or create sanctioned campsites, so this is a policy choice rather than a legal obligation. And Berkeley's own encampment policy already promises a shelter offer before closure whenever practicable, which is a self-imposed standard Council can raise.

suggested.text:
**1. Get Berkeley out of the Flock Safety contract.**

We pay Flock to run license plate readers that photograph our neighbors' cars into a nationwide database. Audits elsewhere found federal agencies, including Border Patrol, searching local Flock data without the cities that owned it knowing; one state's review turned up an undisclosed pilot giving Customs and Border Protection access, and dozens of cities have cancelled. In May 2026 our Peace and Justice Commission recommended cancelling. The Council rejected the roughly $2 million expansion into cameras and drones and renewed the license plate reader contract anyway — twelve months, up to $200,000. That renewal lapses inside the next Council term, which means this seat casts the vote. Our sanctuary ordinance binds every city contractor and carries no criminal carve-out. The contract is the policy, and I would end it.

**2. Finish the storefront policy this Council already started, and fight blight where it is actually getting worse.**

Berkeley already taxes empty homes — Measure M passed with 65% in 2022 and is now billing 863 vacant units — and nothing we have reaches an empty storefront. Our anti-blight ordinance treats vacancy as a nuisance only for residential buildings; a commercial building can sit dark indefinitely so long as the paint holds.

Last December this Council referred a Vibrant Storefront Policy to the City Manager: registration, activation standards, real penalties, a path for pop-ups and community uses. That referral also said that if it does not work, a commercial vacancy tax should go to the ballot. I agree with that sequencing, and my priority is making the first half actually happen — a referral is not an ordinance, and this one has been sitting since December. Registration is the piece we can pass without an election, it makes vacancy visible and costly, and it gives us data we do not currently have.

I would also be careful about the number we are arguing from. Citywide ground-floor vacancy is 6.25%, down from a pandemic peak of 8.4%, and our own economic development staff say 5 to 15 percent is normal market churn. The Downtown Association cites 28%; the City's own measurement for the same year is 10.9%, and the higher figure counts storefronts in buildings slated for demolition. I would rather make an honest case about the corridors that are genuinely getting worse — Telegraph, now above 10% and rising, and San Pablo — than claim a citywide emergency the data does not support.

On the tax itself I would keep the promise modest, because the record is not good. San Francisco's empty homes tax was struck down and enjoined and has collected nothing. Oakland's auditor reported this month that between a quarter and a half of the parcels it noticed as vacant were not vacant, that administration eats about 15% of revenue, and that six years in the City still cannot say whether vacancy fell. Our own empty homes tax sent its first bills 21 months late. So the tax is a fallback with a design problem to solve, not the headline. The goal is filled storefronts — small businesses, nonprofits, childcare, arts and community space with below-market leases and tenant improvement help. If a penalty is what makes that credible, I will vote for it. I am not going to promise it will raise money.

**3. An alternative site for the Harrison Street community — together, not scattered.**

Harrison Street is in the district I am running to represent. It is still occupied. In one fiscal year the city spent nearly $284,000 on outside counsel defending encampment litigation and cleared 40 tons of garbage from the corridor, and the people living there are no closer to housing than they were three years ago. Whatever we are currently doing, it is neither cheap nor working.

Berkeley has run the closest thing to this before. From 2021 to 2022 we operated a transitional village and safe-parking site at 742 Grayson Street, and its residents were mostly people displaced from the RV encampments at 8th and Harrison. It served about 150 people and moved roughly 30 into permanent housing. It did not close because it failed; it closed because the lease ran out.

I would open a site sized to take the Harrison community together. This Council already said it wants that — in May 2025 it passed a referral stating that ideally a site would have capacity to relocate an entire encampment to preserve an existing supportive community — and then staff came back and said not to fund one while existing shelters are closing. They were not wrong about the budget. This year we eliminated the Winter Shelter and cut the STAIR Center by 23%. I would fund it from Measure P, which raises about $11 million a year for exactly this purpose, and from the Encampment Resolution Fund money that must be spent by June 2027 or returned to the state.

I want to be straight about what this is and is not, because the research does not support the way sanctioned sites are usually sold. They are not cheaper than housing people: Portland's cost about $55,000 per unit a year against supportive housing at $16,500 to $22,500 per tenant. There is no rigorous study showing they reduce homelessness — HUD's own review says the evidence is limited and no one has yet compared these programs against what would have happened otherwise. The city-level results flatly contradict each other: Portland found villages beating congregate shelter three to one on permanent-housing exits, while Los Angeles audited its tiny home villages and found the worst return-to-homelessness rate of any shelter type it funds. And the favorable numbers in this field almost always come from the operator or its funder, while the unfavorable ones come from city auditors. And under current federal rules the people living at a sanctioned site are still counted as unsheltered, so a city can spend heavily and show nothing in its own numbers.

So I would not propose this as a solution to homelessness. It is a bridge, and it has to be built as one: funded as a step toward permanent housing rather than a substitute for it, with housing navigation attached from day one, a written expectation of what share of residents reach permanent housing, and a hard commitment that it does not become the destination. The case for it here is narrower and stronger than the national argument — we have a specific community in my district that has been cleared and re-formed repeatedly at real public expense, we have run the model before with the same population, and the alternative on offer is another year of litigation.

Two changes in how we do it. Our encampment policy is detailed about storing property — fourteen days, ninety for anything worth over $100, forty-five minimum for tents and sleeping bags — and silent on pets, partners, and keeping a community together. Berkeley's own evaluation of the 2nd and Cedar closure found residents there had already been swept from somewhere else, and recommended letting people stay with partners, pets, and family. I would write that into the policy. And I would stop pretending the courts are deciding this for us. A federal judge ruled in April that Berkeley is not required to create a sanctioned site. That is the point: it is a choice, and I would make it.

verification.source: Illinois state audit of the Flock CBP pilot; municipal Flock audits reported by NPR and local outlets

State as federal access occurring without city knowledge — not as a single deliberate grant by the company, which the record does not establish.

verification.claim: Berkeley's existing vacancy tax covers residential units only and does not reach commercial property
verification.source: Measure M ballot packet and BMC Chapter 7.54 (Empty Homes Tax)
verification.note: Passed with 64.94% (28,805 to 15,549). BMC 7.54.030(L) defines a Residential Unit; no commercial or non-residential property appears anywhere in Chapter 7.54. Effective January 1, 2024, expires December 31, 2034.

verification.claim: Berkeley's Empty Homes Tax is being implemented and collected
verification.source: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board, Empty Homes Tax Implementation Update; City Manager report amending BMC 7.54
verification.note: First bills issued the week of September 15, 2025 for tax year 2024: 364 properties and 863 units assessed after exemptions, roughly $3.5 to $4 million a year projected. Actual collected revenue is not yet published.

verification.claim: A vacant storefront registry can be adopted by ordinance without a ballot measure
verification.source: San Jose Municipal Code Ch. 17.38 Part 4; comparable registries in Santa Monica, Pasadena, Long Beach, and Richmond
verification.note: Registries rest on police power under California Constitution Article XI Section 7 and Government Code 38771 and recover costs through fees rather than raising revenue, so no vote is required. San Jose's Downtown Registration Area is the only commercial-specific program of either kind in California.

verification.claim: Vacancy taxes have been shown to reduce commercial vacancy
verification.source: Survey of fourteen California cities; Oakland City Auditor performance audit pending
verification.note: No California city has published an official evaluation of effectiveness. Oakland's Measure W has collected an average of $5.9 million a year against roughly $10 million advertised, at 68 to 76 percent collection, and Oakland staff expressly disclaim their assessed-parcel counts as a vacancy metric. In July 2026 Oakland adopted Resolution 91291 removing its own vacancy-tax liens because they were blocking sales of vacant parcels to affordable housing developers. San Diego's Empty Homes Tax failed at the June 2026 ballot, reported at roughly 56.5 percent no — that result is secondary-sourced and the certified totals remain unconfirmed.

verification.claim: The Harrison Street encampment is in District 1 and remains occupied
verification.source: City Manager Public Notice and Order to Abate; Council Item 37 (Kesarwani, District 1); City of Berkeley Public Health Update
verification.note: Harrison Street from 10th to 6th and 8th Street from Gilman to Codornices Creek. The June 10, 2026 update records 40 tons of garbage removed since February 2026 and outreach to occupants, so the site is still occupied. Last primary population figure is 51 people from a 2023 census.

verification.claim: A court requires Berkeley to create a sanctioned campsite
verification.source: Berkeley Homeless Union v. City of Berkeley, No. 3:25-cv-01414-EMC, order on cross-motions for summary judgment (Dkt. 288)
verification.note: The order states the City 'is not required to designate, create, or identify' enforcement-free relocation zones or City-sanctioned campsites. A sanctioned site is legally permitted but not compelled — it is a policy choice. The City did lose on ADA grounds regarding individualized assessment, moving assistance, and property storage.

verification.claim: Shelter capacity is still a legal precondition to closing an encampment
verification.source: City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, 603 U.S. 520 (June 28, 2024), abrogating Martin v. City of Boise
verification.note: Generally applicable camping ordinances may now be enforced even where no shelter beds are available. Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment property protections under Lavan v. City of Los Angeles remain intact, and Grants Pass says nothing about the ADA. Berkeley's own promise of a shelter offer before closure is self-imposed policy under Resolution 71,513-N.S., not a legal floor.

verification.claim: Berkeley has previously operated a sanctioned site serving people displaced from Harrison Street
verification.source: Council Item 29, Alternative Housing Options
verification.note: The Horizon Transitional Village and SPARK safe-parking site at 742 Grayson Street operated July 2021 to October 2022 with up to 40 RVs and about 50 indoor beds, serving roughly 150 people with about 30 connected to permanent housing. Its residents were primarily individuals displaced from the unsanctioned RV encampments at 8th and Harrison. It closed when the City's lease expired, not on performance.

verification.claim: Council has already adopted the goal of relocating an encampment together to preserve its community
verification.source: Council Item 29, Alternative Housing Options; Referral Response, Oct 14, 2025
verification.note: Item 29 states that ideally some sites 'would have capacity to support the relocation of an entire encampment, to preserve an existing supportive community.' It passed as a referral rather than binding policy, and staff responded on October 14, 2025 that absent new external funding they do not recommend opening new programs while existing shelter programs face imminent closure.

verification.claim: Berkeley's adopted encampment policy protects pets, partners, or community cohesion during closures
verification.source: Resolution 71,513-N.S.; Administrative Regulations 10.1 and 10.2
verification.note: The adopted policy and administrative regulations govern notice and property storage — 14 days, 90 days for property with apparent resale value of $100 or more, and a minimum 45 days for tents, tarps, and sleeping bags — but contain no provision on pets, service animals, partners, households, or keeping a community together. That gap is amendable by Council.

verification.claim: Measure P is the revenue a Berkeley councilmember appropriates for homelessness
verification.source: City Manager memo, Measure P and Impact on Homeless Services in Berkeley
verification.note: Real property transfer tax passed November 2018 with 72.4%, raising roughly $11 million a year on average with wide swings by market conditions. In FY26 Berkeley spent $18.9 million on homelessness including $13 million of Measure P. Berkeley is not a direct recipient of state HHAP funds.

verification.claim: The FY2027–28 budget reduced Berkeley's shelter capacity
verification.source: FY2027–FY2028 adopted biennial budget, Resolution 72,340-N.S.
verification.note: The Berkeley Winter Shelter was eliminated for $358,750 in savings, and the STAIR Center took a 23% operating reduction of $400,554 alongside a 25% bed-capacity reduction. The Mayor's supplemental restored other items but not these.

verification.claim: Sanctioned encampments have been shown to reduce homelessness or improve housing outcomes
verification.source: HUD PD&R, Understanding Encampments of People Experiencing Homelessness (Abt Associates); scoping review of tiny homes and sleeping cabins, SSM-Health Systems 2025
verification.note: No randomized, quasi-experimental, or matched-comparison study of sanctioned encampments exists. HUD's own review states 'limited evidence suggests that sanctioned encampments help to reduce homelessness' and that evaluators 'have not yet begun to use methods that compare the results of a response to encampments with what would have happened in the absence of the policy.' The one head-to-head study (CDC Epi-Aid, Denver, n=187) is cross-sectional and measures perceived hazards, not housing or mortality outcomes. Do not claim the model is proven.

verification.claim: Alternative or interim shelter is cheaper per person than permanent supportive housing
verification.source: Portland State University Homelessness Research & Action Collaborative, Alternative Shelter Evaluation Report (Multnomah County); Los Angeles City Controller, Pathways to Permanent Housing
verification.note: Portland operating cost per unit per year: congregate $20,386, villages $30,927, motels $43,401, Safe Rest Villages $55,000 — against supportive housing at $16,500 to $22,500 per tenant year. Los Angeles non-congregate interim runs about $57,000 per bed per year. Village capital costs are lower only where land is free and pod replacement is excluded. The cost argument for sanctioned sites does not survive contact with the two jurisdictions that actually account for it.

verification.claim: HUD counts residents of sanctioned sites as sheltered in the Point-in-Time count
verification.source: HUD Point-in-Time count classification, as applied to Phoenix Safe Outdoor Space
verification.note: Residents of sanctioned outdoor sites are counted as unsheltered even where the site has 24/7 staffing, meals, showers, and housing navigation. A city can therefore spend upward of $50,000 per person per year and record no reduction in its reported unsheltered count. This is a real governance consequence a council should legislate around rather than discover afterward.

verification.claim: Encampment Resolution Fund outcomes have been evaluated by the state
verification.source: California State Auditor, Report 2023-102.1, Homelessness in California
verification.note: The Auditor could not assess ERF cost-effectiveness: four of ten grantees reviewed submitted incomplete or unusable outcome data, with some entering 'data not collected' or leaving fields blank, and Cal ICH relies on unverified self-certified grantee data. Berkeley's ERF Round 3 award is still the right money to spend by June 2027, but its results should be measured locally rather than assumed.

verification.claim: Berkeley's Council has already acted on commercial vacancy and chose the sequencing
verification.source: Council Item 33, Referral to the City Manager and City Attorney: Vibrant Storefront Policy; Annotated Agenda, Dec. 2, 2025
verification.note: Council approved a referral to develop a Vibrant Storefront Policy — registration and activation performance standards, two activation pathways, per-day penalties, an appeals process, and a 90-day effective date. The same referral names a commercial vacancy tax as the explicit fallback: if the storefront policy does not reduce vacancies, Council 'may consider developing a commercial vacancy tax to be placed on ballot for a future election.' A candidate position has to engage with that sequencing rather than propose it fresh.

verification.claim: Berkeley's commercial vacancy rate is at crisis levels
verification.source: City Manager, Berkeley Economic Dashboards Update, Council Worksession
verification.note: Citywide ground-floor commercial vacancy by square footage peaked at 8.4% in 2022 and fell to 6.25% in 2025, against 5.0% in 2018. The Office of Economic Development's own standing footnote states that typical district vacancy runs 5 to 15 percent from natural market churn, so the citywide figure sits near the bottom of the range OED calls normal. The districts actually rising are Telegraph, 9.9% to 10.45%, and San Pablo, 7.1% to 8.44%; Downtown fell to 9.68%. Argue the corridors, not a citywide crisis.

verification.claim: Downtown Berkeley storefront vacancy is roughly 28 percent
verification.source: Downtown Berkeley Association Strategic Plan versus City of Berkeley Office of Economic Development dashboard
verification.note: The Downtown Berkeley Association reports vacancy climbing 'as high as 28%' and the December 2025 Council referral cites 28.2% for 2024; the City's own OED figure for the same year is 10.9%. Both are primary sources measuring different boundaries and inclusion rules, and the higher figure counts storefronts in buildings scheduled for demolition. Do not use 28% without that caveat.

verification.claim: A residential vacancy tax of this design has survived legal challenge in California
verification.source: Debbane v. City and County of San Francisco, SF Superior Court No. CGC-23-604600; San Francisco Ordinance No. 41-25
verification.note: San Francisco's Empty Homes Tax was held to violate the federal and state constitutions and to be preempted by California law; the City is enjoined from enforcing it, has collected $0, and suspended the tax retroactive to January 1, 2024 pending appeal (No. A172067, First District). Ellis Act preemption reaches residential property only and would not touch a commercial tax, but the takings, due process, and equal protection theories are not residential-specific. Confirm the appellate status before any public statement.

verification.claim: Vacancy taxes are administratively straightforward to collect
verification.source: Oakland City Auditor, Performance Audit of the Vacant Property Tax; San Francisco Treasurer and Tax Collector CVT return instructions
verification.note: Oakland's auditor found that between 26% and 49% of parcels noticed as vacant each year were not vacant, that administration has averaged about 15% of revenue and reached 28% in year one, and that the City still cannot say whether the tax reduced vacancy. In San Francisco more than half the commercial tax base never files at all — 52% to 59% of parcels across 2022 to 2024. Berkeley's own Empty Homes Tax issued first bills 21 months late and required an amending ordinance to fix first-cycle problems.

verification.claim: A commercial vacancy tax would be passed through to tenants as higher rents
verification.source: Moszkowski and Stackman, Option Value and Storefront Vacancy in New York City
verification.note: A tax on holding space empty lowers the landlord's outside option rather than raising the cost of an occupied tenancy; the modeled effect is average rents falling about 0.44%. This is the easiest pro-tax claim for opponents to break and the easiest anti-tax claim to rebut — do not argue pass-through in either direction. The stronger economic objection is the welfare threshold, and that most vacancy is transitory: only 12.5% of Oakland's vacant parcels were vacant all six years.

verification.claim: The observational evidence on village-style shelter points the same way across cities
verification.source: Portland State University HRAC Alternative Shelter Evaluation; Los Angeles City Controller, Pathways to Permanent Housing; Oakland City Auditor, Performance Audit of Homelessness Services
verification.note: Portland found villages reaching 36% permanent-housing exits against 11% for congregate shelter. Los Angeles found tiny home villages its worst performer at 2% to 18%, with 76% exiting to homelessness or unknown. Oakland's cabins hit 27% to 31% against a 50% target. All three used HMIS and none adjusted for who was placed where. Citing Portland without Los Angeles is cherry-picking, and the likeliest explanation for the gap is population and voucher availability rather than the shelter form.

verification.claim: The favorable and unfavorable findings in this literature come from comparable sources
verification.source: Comparison of source provenance across Seattle, Denver, Portland, Oakland, Los Angeles, San Francisco, and the California State Auditor
verification.note: Every favorable headline figure traces to an operator or its funder — Seattle's 46% to a mayoral press release citing KCRHA, whose financial controls were later found deficient; its 53% to the operator; Denver's 58% to the operator's own unaudited annual report using an undefined 'positive housing' category. Every unfavorable figure comes from an independent auditor: Oakland's City Auditor, LA's Controller, Portland's City Auditor, San Francisco's Controller, and the California State Auditor. State that asymmetry rather than averaging across it.

verification.claim: Cities that pioneered sanctioned outdoor sites have kept them
verification.source: Colorado Village Collaborative annual report; San Francisco Controller, Assessment of the San Francisco Shelter System
verification.note: Denver wound down its final Safe Outdoor Space in January 2025 and converted the model to hard-sided micro-communities. San Francisco's safe sleeping program was a pandemic response and has closed. Both were retired by their own operators without ever receiving an independent outcome evaluation.

verification.claim: Safe parking specifically has peer-reviewed evaluation behind it

questions.analysis: Repealing the Ellis Act requires state legislation; a councilmember can advocate but not vote. questions.question: Do you support repealing Costa Hawkins?
questions.analysis: Repealing Costa-Hawkins requires state action, but for Berkeley the consequences are unusually concrete: the municipal code already contains dormant standby provisions written to activate on repeal. BMC 13.76.100(D) restores a rent ceiling at the most recent lawfully established rent if state law stops mandating that landlords set initial rents, which ends vacancy decontrol going forward. BMC 13.76.050(B)(1) converts the permanent post-June-1980 new-construction exemption into a rolling fifteen-year exemption. BMC 13.76.050(B)(2) self-terminates by its own terms, bringing single-family homes and condominiums under full coverage. Roughly 20,000 Berkeley units currently have regulated rents. The candidate can therefore answer this question with specific local mechanics rather than general support.

suggested.text:
Yes.

Costa-Hawkins is the reason Berkeley's rent stabilization ordinance protects a tenancy but not a unit. Because of it, a landlord resets rent to market the moment a tenant leaves, and everything built after June 1980 is permanently exempt. Over 20,000 Berkeley units have regulated rents, and state law caps what that regulation can actually do.

Repeal is not abstract for Berkeley. Our voters already wrote the follow-on provisions into our own code, waiting for state law to get out of the way. On repeal, Chapter 13.76 restores rent ceilings at the most recent lawful rent, ending vacancy decontrol; the permanent exemption for post-1980 construction becomes a rolling fifteen-year exemption, so newer buildings come under control as they age; and the single-family exemption ends by its own terms. I support repeal, and I would make sure the Rent Board has implementation guidance ready the day it happens rather than months after.

questions.question: Do you support policies that would ban the use of price setting algorithms in the housing market? (ie. Realpage)
questions.analysis: Berkeley has already legislated here, and the legislative history matters more than the headline. Ordinance 7,956-N.S. added BMC Chapter 13.63 and was adopted March 25, 2025, effective April 24, 2025. RealPage sued in RealPage, Inc. v. City of Berkeley (N.D. Cal. 3:25-cv-03004-JSC) on First Amendment grounds; the City agreed not to enforce pending the preliminary-injunction motion and Ordinance 7,974-N.S. suspended the effective date. Ordinance 7,992-N.S., adopted December 2, 2025, deleted the suspension and substantially narrowed the prohibition: 'competitor data' now reaches only information not available to the general public, about properties the landlord does not own or manage, and less than 90 days old, with carve-outs for appraisal, project financing, and machine-learning model training. The narrowed ordinance is in force, carrying penalties up to $1,000 per violation per unit per month plus a private right of action. Describing Berkeley as having banned RealPage without that history would overstate what survived. Note also that the California WFP claims banning AI-enabled price fixing as one of its own policy wins, so this is a question the organization follows closely.

levers.text: Defend and, if litigation permits, restore the broader scope Ordinance 7,956-N.S. originally had
Fund City Attorney enforcement of BMC 13.63 so the private right of action is not the only remedy in practice
Support state and federal action against algorithmic price coordination in rental housing

City Attorney report — Amendments to Ordinance Prohibiting the Sale or Use of Coordinated Pricing Algorithms
Annotated Agenda — Council, December 2, 2025 (Ordinance 7,992-N.S. second reading)

suggested.text:
Yes. Berkeley has already done it, and I would defend it.

When landlords feed their rents into shared pricing software, they stop competing and start coordinating. The tenant sees a market rate; what they are actually seeing is a recommendation every nearby landlord received at once.

Berkeley adopted Chapter 13.63 in March 2025 to prohibit exactly that. RealPage sued on First Amendment grounds, the city suspended enforcement, and in December 2025 the Council adopted a narrower version that is in force today — it now reaches non-public competitor data less than 90 days old, with carve-outs for appraisals and model training. It still carries penalties of up to $1,000 per unit per month and lets tenants sue directly.

I would rather have the narrower ordinance standing than a broader one enjoined. But I do not think the current line is where it should permanently sit, and I would support restoring scope as the litigation allows, alongside state action so that no single city has to absorb this fight alone.

A CalGEM WellSTAR spatial query over Berkeley returns zero oil, gas, and geothermal wells; Alameda County as a whole holds 100 wells, of which 92 are plugged, 7 canceled, and 1 idle, with none active or producing, and the state's 2023 Annual Report records zero production for the county. No designated oil field boundary and no well stimulation record intersects Berkeley. A setback ordinance would therefore regulate nothing here, and the honest local statement is that no well has ever been drilled within city limits rather than that Berkeley prohibits drilling.

levers.text: Support statewide setback requirements between extraction sites and homes, schools, and hospitals
Amend BMC 23.502.020 to prohibit commercial oil and gas extraction outright rather than allow it by use permit

sources.label: CalGEM WellSTAR Wells GIS service
CalGEM — California State Oil and Gas Supervisor Annual Report 2023

suggested.text:
Yes.

There has never been an oil or gas well drilled inside Berkeley, and there is no active production anywhere in Alameda County, so a setback here would not move a single rig. I support the statewide standard regardless, because the communities that carry this burden — in Kern County, in Wilmington, in South Los Angeles — are breathing the consequences of a siting pattern that was never accidental.

There is one thing I can do locally. Berkeley's zoning code still lists drilling for oil or natural gas as a conditional use available by permit in our manufacturing and commercial districts. Nobody has ever applied, but the door is legally open. I would close it.

questions.question: Do you support ending all new oil and gas wells in California?
questions.analysis: A statewide question with no local permitting dimension, since Berkeley contains no wells and issues no drilling permits. Worth distinguishing from the candidate's most recognizable local climate lever: Berkeley's natural gas ban in new construction (Ordinance 7,672-N.S., BMC Chapter 12.80) was held preempted by the federal Energy Policy and Conservation Act in California Restaurant Association v. City of Berkeley and was repealed by Ordinance 7,907-N.S. on June 4, 2024. Citing that ban as current law would be a factual error. What is in force is the Building Emissions Saving Ordinance, BMC Chapter 19.81, amended April 15, 2025 and effective January 1, 2026.

levers.text: Support state legislation ending new oil and gas well permits
Implement and strengthen the Building Emissions Saving Ordinance as the operative local decarbonization tool

suggested.text:
Yes. California should stop permitting new oil and gas wells.

Berkeley has none to permit, so my record on this is about buildings rather than wellheads. I want to be straight about that record: Berkeley passed the country's first natural gas ban in new construction in 2019, the Ninth Circuit held it preempted by federal appliance law, and the Council repealed it in June 2024. I would rather say that plainly than claim a law we no longer have.

What we do have is the Building Emissions Saving Ordinance, which took effect this January and requires efficiency improvements at time of sale. I would fund its implementation, and pursue an all-electric reach code within whatever room the preemption ruling and AB 130 actually leave us.

questions.question: Do you support allocating more state funding for public transit?
questions.analysis: A state budget question. The local connection is concrete: Berkeley's FY2027–FY2031 Capital Improvement Program identifies roughly $59.75 million in 2026 dollars of citywide transit improvements — bus-only lanes, queue-jump lanes, and transit signal priority — that are largely unfunded. Berkeley adopted a Transit-First Policy Implementation Plan as Resolution 70,751-N.S. on March 21, 2023 and in the same action seated councilmembers on a quarterly Inter-Agency Liaison Committee with AC Transit. State operating support is also the binding constraint on service levels the City cannot itself fund.

levers.text: Support state operating and capital funding for transit districts
Appropriate Measure B/BB local return funds toward the unfunded transit capital projects in the CIP
Use the Transit-First Implementation Plan and the AC Transit liaison committee to prioritize bus speed on city streets

sources.label: Annotated Agenda — Council, March 21, 2023 (Resolution 70,751-N.S., Transit-First Policy Implementation Plan)
City of Berkeley — Public Transit

suggested.text:
Yes.

Transit in the Bay Area is facing an operating cliff, and no amount of local goodwill closes it. AC Transit and BART are independent districts with their own boards and their own farebox math; when state operating support falls short, service gets cut, and the riders who lose a route are the ones least able to drive instead.

Berkeley has already identified about $59.75 million in transit priority work — bus-only lanes, queue jumps, signal priority — in our capital plan, and most of it is unfunded. That is the piece I would actually control: the streets themselves. I would direct our Measure B and BB local return dollars toward making buses faster through Berkeley, and use our seat on the AC Transit liaison committee to make sure our street projects match where their service actually needs help.

Purchase AC Transit EasyPass for a resident group beyond city employees, as Berkeley already does for staff

And the current programs are less generous than they are often described: AC Transit youth fares are half price, not free, and the free student pass in Berkeley is county Measure BB money that our school district makes available only to families who qualify for free or reduced-price meals — while Emery Unified and Livermore Valley offer it to every student.

That last one is a vote I would actually hold. Berkeley has a seat on the Alameda County Transportation Commission, which runs that program, and I would use it to make the pass universal for every Berkeley Unified student. Locally, our General Plan has directed the City to consider a citywide transit pass since 2001 and we have never funded it. questions.question: Will you commit to working to reduce rates of incarceration?
questions.analysis: Authority here is split in a way that a flat answer usually gets wrong in both directions. Berkeley does operate a jail — the Berkeley Public Safety Center, a Type I facility housing up to 40 detainees between arrest and arraignment, administered by the Police Department — so the claim that Berkeley has no jail is false. What Berkeley does not control is prosecution, pretrial detention beyond arraignment, sentencing custody, or conditions at Santa Rita Jail, all of which sit with Alameda County's elected Sheriff and District Attorney and the Board of Supervisors, on which Berkeley has no vote. Council did adopt a Care First, Jails Last policy by Resolution 71,007-N.S. in July 2023, requiring departmental policy revisions and semiannual reporting to Council on transports to diversion versus jail; whether those reports have been filed could not be confirmed.

levers.text: Set arrest, booking, citation-in-lieu, and diversion policy through the Police Department budget and policy manual
Enforce the semiannual Care First, Jails Last reporting requirement already adopted by Council
Press the Alameda County Board of Supervisors and Sheriff on Santa Rita Jail population and conditions

sources.label: City of Berkeley — Berkeley City Jail

suggested.text:
Yes.

I want to be precise about the levers, because this is an area where city candidates often promise things counties decide. Berkeley runs a jail — a 40-bed facility that holds people between arrest and arraignment. Everything after that point, including Santa Rita, belongs to the county Sheriff, the District Attorney, and the Board of Supervisors, where Berkeley has no vote.

So the honest commitment is about the front door, which is entirely ours: who gets arrested rather than cited, which calls get a clinician instead of a squad car, and whether diversion exists at the moment of contact. Berkeley adopted a Care First, Jails Last policy in 2023 that requires the Police Chief and our Mental Health division to report to Council twice a year on how many people are transported to diversion versus to jail. I could not find evidence those reports have been filed. Making that reporting real is where I would start, because we cannot reduce something we have stopped counting.

questions.question: Will you invest in non-police emergency response systems?
questions.analysis: Berkeley has moved backwards on this within the last two months, and the answer must reflect that. The Specialized Care Unit — a three-person team of a peer support specialist, an EMT, and a clinician, operated under contract by Bonita House and reached at its own phone line — ran from September 5, 2023 to May 2025 and is recorded as complete in the City's Reimagining Public Safety status update. It was funded entirely with one-time money: $4.75 million in ARPA, a $536,500 DHCS grant that expired June 30, 2025, and $68,000 in MHSA, with the City Manager's April 2025 memo stating plainly that there is no recurring funding. Then the budget adopted June 23, 2026 eliminated the 2.6 remaining FTE of the Mobile Crisis Team, described in the budget document as the last General Fund–funded mental health crisis response positions, with responsibility for wellness checks and psychiatric emergencies shifting solely to the Police Department. BerkDOT was never created: the July 2020 action was a referral to the City Manager, it is classified as paused and defunded at Tier 3, and traffic and parking enforcement both remain inside the Police Department. Any answer premised on Berkeley currently having non-police crisis response would be false.

levers.text: Restore General Fund positions for mental health crisis response eliminated in the FY2027–28 budget
Fund a successor to the Specialized Care Unit with recurring rather than one-time money
Revive the BerkDOT referral and move traffic enforcement out of the Police Department to the extent state law permits
Press Alameda County to ensure its Medi-Cal mobile crisis system actually covers Berkeley call volume

sources.label: City of Berkeley — Reimagining Public Safety, Summer 2025 Status Update

City of Berkeley — Crisis Services

suggested.text:
Yes — and in Berkeley that now means rebuilding something we just dismantled.

Berkeley ran a Specialized Care Unit from September 2023 to May 2025: a peer counselor, an EMT, and a clinician who answered mental health and substance use calls without a police officer. It worked, and it was funded entirely with one-time federal and grant money. When that ran out, it ended. Then the budget adopted this June eliminated the last 2.6 city-funded mental health crisis positions. The budget document says it directly: the City will no longer provide crisis response services, and wellness checks and psychiatric emergencies now fall solely to the Berkeley Police Department.

I would not have voted for that. Sending an armed officer to a psychiatric emergency is a choice, and we made it because a pilot was never given a permanent budget line. I would restore those positions and fund a successor to the SCU out of ongoing General Fund money rather than the next grant cycle. I would also revive BerkDOT, which Berkeley has described as a priority since 2020 without ever creating it — traffic and parking enforcement still sit inside the police department.

One thing I will not do is describe our police budget as shrinking. It is not. All-funds police spending rises by about $661,000 next year. Reductions measured against a projection are not reductions.

questions.question:
What describes your commitment to supporting sanctuary policies for immigrants by prohibiting collaboration between ICE and local law enforcement?
For all cases
With exceptions granted for limited violent felonies ie. sexual assault of minor, domestic violence and homicide.
I do not support sanctuary city policies.
Other: Please Explain
questions.analysis: This is a multiple-choice question where Berkeley's actual ordinance supports the strongest option without qualification. Ordinance 7,984-N.S., adding BMC Chapter 13.114, was adopted on second reading September 30, 2025 and contains no criminal offense carve-out — no serious or violent felony list, no Penal Code 1192.7 or 667.5 exception. Its only exceptions are consent, service provision, and what state or federal law compels. This matters because state law leaves that discretion open: Government Code 7282.5 permits, but does not require, cooperation for a long list of offenses, and expressly conditions it on not violating local policy. Berkeley closes that door. Police Department Policy 415 reproduces the ordinance and states that members 'shall not transfer an individual to immigration authorities.' Berkeley also goes beyond SB 54 by binding every City agency and contractor, requiring written reporting of every ICE request to Council within ten business days, and restricting consent searches of non-public City property. Two cautions: a January 2025 council report miscites the 1986 sanctuary resolution number, and Policy 415.7.5 retains residual template language about reporting transfers that contradicts the flat prohibition — not an operative carve-out, but a hostile questioner could point at it.

levers.text: Defend and enforce BMC Chapter 13.114, including the ten-business-day Council reporting requirement
Direct removal of the residual transfer-reporting language in Police Policy 415.7.5 that conflicts with the ordinance
Use BMC Chapter 13.105 contracting restrictions to keep City procurement clear of data brokers serving immigration enforcement
Reconsider the automated license plate reader contract extended in May 2026 over the Peace and Justice Commission's objection

sources.label: Proposed Sanctuary City Ordinance — Council Referral (Ordinance 7,984-N.S. text)
Annotated Agenda — Council, September 30, 2025 (second reading adopted)
California Government Code § 7282.5

suggested.text:
For all cases.

Berkeley's sanctuary ordinance, adopted in September 2025, contains no criminal carve-out at all. Our police may not transfer anyone to immigration authorities, full stop, and may notify only on an outstanding criminal warrant. That was a deliberate choice. State law under SB 54 leaves cities discretion to cooperate on a long list of offenses — but it conditions that discretion on local policy, and Berkeley's policy closes it.

I support that, and I would defend it. A carve-out is not a narrow exception in practice; it is a reason for every immigrant in the city to assume that calling the police is a risk. The moment cooperation is conditional, the protection stops working for everyone.

Our ordinance also does things SB 54 does not: it binds every city department and contractor rather than just police, and it requires any ICE request to be reported to the Council in writing within ten business days. I would make sure that reporting actually happens, and I would keep our procurement clear of vendors that sell data into immigration enforcement.

verification.note: No criminal-offense carve-out exists — no serious or violent felony list and no Penal Code 1192.7 or 667.5 exception. Policy 415.7.4 states members 'shall not transfer an individual to immigration authorities'; notification is limited to an outstanding criminal warrant.

questions.question: Will you reject campaign contributions and endorsements from oil companies, oil company associations, public utilities and PAC's which take money from any of the above including but not limited to: Chevron, Valero, Western States Petroleum Association, and Sempra Energy?
questions.analysis: Part of a block of six pledge questions. Berkeley's answer is unusually strong because local law already forbids most of what is being asked about: BMC 2.12.440, part of the Berkeley Election Reform Act, prohibits any proprietorship, firm, partnership, joint venture, syndicate, business trust, company, corporation including non-profit corporations, or labor union from contributing to any candidate, and bars campaign treasurers from soliciting or accepting such contributions. Separately, participation in Berkeley's Public Financing Program caps every contribution at $60 and bars contributions from political action committees. questions.question: What distinguishes you as a Working Families Party candidate from your opponents?
questions.analysis: A comparative question. The distinction WFP looks for is structural — funding sources, base of support, and accountability to organizations — rather than differences in stated positions, since in Berkeley most candidates will state similar ones. The answer runs on three claims, each independently checkable. First, the surveillance contract: on May 7, 2026 the Council declined the Peace and Justice Commission's recommendation to cancel Berkeley's Flock Safety contracts, rejected a roughly $2 million expansion into cameras and drones, and adopted Resolution 72,254-N.S. renewing the automated license plate reader contract twelve months for up to $200,000 — so the expansion was stopped and the underlying contract was not, and the renewal lapses inside the next Council term. Second, the sanctuary claim: Berkeley's ordinance, BMC Chapter 13.114, contains no criminal carve-out and binds every City agency and contractor, which is what makes a procurement decision a sanctuary question rather than a separate one. Third, campaign structure: BMC 2.12.440 already bars corporate, business-entity, and union contributions to any Berkeley candidate, and the public financing program caps contributions at $60 and bars PAC money outright, so the independence claim is a legal fact about the campaign rather than a promise. Note that another Berkeley candidate has run on ending the Flock contract, so this is a shared position in the field and the distinction has to rest on more than holding it.

suggested.text:
Three things, and the first is why I am in this race at all.

**The contract.** Berkeley pays Flock Safety to run automated license plate readers that photograph our neighbors' cars and feed a nationwide database. Audits elsewhere have since found federal agencies, including Border Patrol, searching local Flock data without the cities that owned it knowing — one state's review turned up an undisclosed pilot giving Customs and Border Protection access, and dozens of cities have cancelled since. In May 2026 our Council had the chance to end it. The Peace and Justice Commission recommended cancelling. The Council rejected the roughly $2 million expansion into cameras and drones — good — and renewed the license plate reader contract anyway, twelve more months and up to $200,000. Half a decision. That renewal lapses during the next Council term, so whoever holds this seat casts the vote.

**Why it is a sanctuary question, not a procurement one.** Berkeley's sanctuary ordinance binds every city agency, employee, and contractor, and carries no criminal carve-out. We wrote it that way on purpose. A city cannot promise its immigrant residents that it will not hand over information and then pay a vendor whose database federal agents have been searching without our knowledge. The contract is the policy. I would vote to end it, and until that vote comes I would condition it on audit rights and a hard bar on federal access.

**Why I can say that without hedging.** I am running in Berkeley's public financing program. Under our Election Reform Act no corporation, business entity, or union may contribute to any candidate here; under public financing no contribution to me may exceed $60 and no political action committee may give at all. My campaign is small-dollar neighbors and a public match. Nobody holding a city contract has a stake in how I vote on city contracts.

I would not claim to be the only candidate who wants Berkeley out of this contract — I am not, and that is a good thing. The distinction I would draw is that I did not arrive at it from a policy platform. I arrived at the race from this.
